title: Markdowns in Seasonal Conspicuous Goods
abstract: In common parlance, luxury and markdowns are, in many respects, contradictory concepts. Markdowns decrease product exclusivity and hence consumers’ willingness to pay (i.e., snob effect) since most consumers purchasing luxury desire uniqueness. Markdowns also encourage strategic (forward-looking) consumers to wait for lower prices (i.e., strategic effect). Yet, luxury retailers frequently adopt markdowns in practice to stimulate the demand for their seasonal products (i.e., sales effect). To study the impact of these three countervailing effects on a luxury retailer’s markdown policy and rationing strategy, this paper develops a game-theoretic model with strategic and exclusivity-seeking consumers who have heterogeneous (high and low) valuations. We characterize a luxury retailer’s equilibrium markdown and rationing strategies, and find that the retailer induces a buying frenzy (i.e., selling deliberately less than the demand) to increase consumers’ willingness to pay when they are sufficiently exclusivity-seeking. We show that the retailer’s markdown policy depends on consumers’ desire for exclusivity when the proportion of consumers with high valuation is not too high or too low. Interestingly, we find that, in such cases, consumers’ higher desire for exclusivity does not motivate the retailer to increase exclusivity and to adopt uniform pricing. To the contrary, it motivates the retailer to decrease the exclusivity and to adopt markdowns. By doing so, we identify exclusivity-seeking consumer behavior as another rationale behind markdown pricing. Lastly, we find that, when selling to exclusivity-seeking consumers, the negative impact of strategic consumer behavior is lower; however, ignoring it can be more costly.

summary.oneLiner: A game-theoretic model shows exclusivity-seeking shoppers can make luxury retailers mark prices down and ration stock, reversing the usual intuition that luxury avoids markdowns.
summary.overview: Luxury retailers often mark down seasonal products, even though markdowns seem to conflict with exclusivity. The authors build a two-period game-theoretic model in which a retailer sells to strategic buyers (who may wait for a lower price) and snobbish buyers (who value being among the first with a unique product). They find that when buyers strongly want exclusivity, the retailer may deliberately sell less than demand to raise willingness to pay, and that markdowns can be optimal when the share of high-valuation buyers is low or intermediate. The paper also finds that ignoring strategic waiting behavior can be costly when buyers seek exclusivity.
summary.question: When should a luxury retailer adopt markdowns, what role does exclusivity-seeking consumer behavior play in the markdown and rationing strategy, and how does strategic consumer behavior affect the retailer's profit when selling to exclusivity-seeking consumers?
summary.method: A game-theoretic model in which a profit-maximising monopoly retailer chooses order quantity and prices over two periods, with strategic and snobbish consumers who have high or low valuations. The model is solved by backward induction and characterised analytically, supported by numerical examples and comparisons with myopic consumers and with non-snobbish consumers.
summary.data: No empirical sample. The study uses a theoretical model with parameter values chosen for illustration (for example, vH = 15, vL = 4, c = 1). Real-world examples from retailers such as Barneys New York, Farfetch and Nordstrom are cited as illustrations, based on the authors' casual observations of websites.
findings: When consumers are not exclusivity-seeking, the retailer never marks prices down and does not induce a buying frenzy.
With sufficiently exclusivity-seeking consumers, the retailer rations and induces a buying frenzy to increase consumers' willingness to pay.
Exclusivity-seeking consumer behavior leads to price markdowns when the proportion of high-value consumers is sufficiently low.
When the proportion of high-value consumers is intermediate, higher desire for exclusivity can motivate the retailer to decrease exclusivity and adopt markdowns.

The negative impact of strategic consumer behavior on profit is lower with exclusivity-seeking consumers, but ignoring strategic behavior can be more costly, decreasing profit by up to 45% in the numerical example.
The authors describe these results as suggestive of the model's logic and consistent with some observed luxury retail practices.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest that luxury retailers should not automatically avoid markdowns, and that markdown decisions should depend on the share of high-valuation customers and on how strongly customers seek exclusivity. They suggest that limited editions and waiting lists can be rationing tools that raise willingness to pay. They also argue that retailers should account for strategic customers who wait for lower prices, since ignoring them can be costly.
